title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 18: Firestone Ceramics v. Court of Appeals -- Sauce for the Poor Goose: A Postscript
keywords: Firestone Ceramics v. Court of Appeals
Sauce for the Poor Goose: A Postscript
primary_topics: Chapter 18 of 'A Centenary of Justice' -- a short postscript completing the critique CJP began in Chapter 22 of his earlier book 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity': that the en banc's elevation (8-7) of a Third Division decision in Firestone Ceramics v. Court of Appeals was inappropriate because the losing movants 'utterly failed to adduce any legal reason for such referral'

The follow-up ruling: on January 30, 2001 the full Court UNANIMOUSLY denied the petitioner-movants' Motion for Reconsideration and upheld the Third Division's own unanimous original decision -- vindicating, in CJP's view, the very Division whose case had been 'yanked' to the banc

The merits the Court reaffirmed: res judicata via the Margolles case (substantial, not absolute, identity of parties suffices; the parties were 'privy in law'); the burden of proving the nullity of a 70-year-old Torrens title (OCT No. 4216) rests on the petitioner; and the State faced no real loss of patrimony, since reverted land 'would not be devoted to public use' but reserved for disposition to private persons

CJP's institutional point: the banc's takeover of a Division case for which no legal reason was shown 'merely resulted in a waste of precious time' and 'uselessly and imprudently clogged the Court's dockets' -- the lesson of the maxim 'Sauce for the poor goose should be the same sauce for the rich gander'
sub_topics: The backstory: Chapter 22 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' (2000) criticized the en banc's 8-7 decision to 'yank' the Firestone Ceramics cases 'out of and against the will of' the Third Division and treat them as banc cases, even though the losing movants gave no legal reason for the referral (CJP was among the seven dissenters)
The unanimous reconsideration: on January 30, 2001 the full Court denied the Motion for Reconsideration and upheld the Third Division's unanimous original decision after oral argument

Ground 1 -- res judicata via Margolles: although Firestone was not a party to the Margolles case, 'absolute identity of parties is not required but only substantial identity'; Firestone's claim and the Margolles losing parties' claim raised 'exactly the same argument' against OCT No. 4216 (that it covered unclassified forest land, so the 1929 land-registration court lacked jurisdiction over the Gana spouses' application), making them 'privy in law'

Ground 2 -- burden of proof: the presumption that registered land was public domain had to be overcome in the original 1927 proceedings and is legally presumed satisfied by the decree; in an action to annul that judgment as void, 'the burden of proving the nullity rests with the petitioner'

Ground 3 -- no loss of State patrimony: reverting the land to the government would not devote it to public use but 'reserve it for eventual disposition to other private persons' (notably Firestone itself); annulling 70-year-old Torrens titles only to re-dispose the land 'would betray a subservience to technicality' -- 'a simple matter of equity and good sense'

CJP's rationale for inclusion and the docket-clogging critique: the chapter 'complete[s] and put[s] to rest' Chapter 22 of 'Transparency'; the unanimous January 30 Resolution showed 'the folly' of ignoring the maxim that 'Sauce for the poor goose should be the same sauce for the rich gander,' since the banc's inappropriate takeover 'uselessly and imprudently clogged the Court's dockets'

stances.claim: The en banc's elevation of the Firestone Ceramics cases out of the Third Division -- over the Division's will and without any legal reason shown by the losing movants -- was inappropriate; the unanimous January 30, 2001 denial of reconsideration (upholding the Division's own unanimous decision) proved that the takeover 'merely resulted in a waste of precious time' and 'uselessly and imprudently clogged the Court's dockets.' Sauce for the poor goose should be the same sauce for the rich gander.
stances.rhetorical_move: vindication-by-outcome plus the poor-goose maxim: using the banc's eventual unanimous agreement with the Division to show the takeover was a needless, docket-clogging departure from even-handed practice
stances.confidence: asserted as CJP's institutional critique (he was among the seven dissenters)

stances.claim: On the merits, the Court of Appeals correctly denied annulment of the title: res judicata applied through the Margolles case because 'absolute identity of parties is not required but only substantial identity' -- Firestone and the Margolles losing parties raised the same argument against OCT No. 4216, making them 'privy in law' -- the burden of proving a 70-year-old decree void rests on the petitioner, and reverting the land would only re-dispose it to private persons, not serve public use: 'a simple matter of equity and good sense.'
stances.rhetorical_move: substantial-identity res judicata plus equity: closing off relitigation by privity of interest and reframing reversion as technicality that serves no public purpose
stances.confidence: the Court's unanimous holding on reconsideration

notable_anecdotes: The case that was 'yanked': CJP recounts that the en banc, by a one-vote 8-7 margin, pulled the Firestone Ceramics cases 'out of and against the will of' the Third Division and treated them as banc cases -- even though the losing movants had given no legal reason for the referral.

Vindication of the Division: the same full Court that took over the cases ended up unanimously denying reconsideration and upholding the Third Division's own unanimous original decision -- the outcome CJP cites to show the takeover changed nothing but the docket load.

The poor goose and the rich gander: CJP frames the whole episode around the maxim 'Sauce for the poor goose should be the same sauce for the rich gander,' arguing that special banc treatment for a well-resourced litigant's case, absent any legal ground, is exactly the inconsistency the saying warns against.

Reversion that helps no one public: the Court noted that if the disputed land were reverted to the government it 'would not be devoted to public use' but reserved for disposition to private persons -- indeed to Firestone itself -- so annulling 70-year-old titles would be 'subservience to technicality,' not service of the national patrimony.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 18 of 'A Centenary of Justice' is a short postscript completing a critique CJP began in Chapter 22 of his earlier book 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity': that the Supreme Court en banc, by a one-vote 8-7 margin, had inappropriately pulled the Firestone Ceramics v. Court of Appeals cases 'out of and against the will of' its Third Division and treated them as banc cases, even though the losing movants 'utterly failed to adduce any legal reason for such referral.' He now reports the sequel: on January 30, 2001 the full Court UNANIMOUSLY denied the movants' Motion for Reconsideration and upheld the Third Division's own unanimous original decision. On the merits, the Court reaffirmed that the Court of Appeals correctly refused to annul the title -- res judicata applied through the Margolles case because 'absolute identity of parties is not required but only substantial identity,' Firestone and the Margolles losing parties having raised the same argument against OCT No. 4216 (that it covered forest land so the 1929 registration court lacked jurisdiction over the Gana spouses), making them 'privy in law'; the burden of proving a 70-year-old decree void rests on the petitioner; and the State faced no real loss of patrimony, since reverted land 'would not be devoted to public use' but reserved for disposition to private persons, including Firestone itself -- 'a simple matter of equity and good sense.' CJP's purpose in including the piece is institutional: the unanimous outcome showed 'the folly' of ignoring the maxim that 'Sauce for the poor goose should be the same sauce for the rich gander,' since the banc's needless takeover 'merely resulted in a waste of precious time' and 'uselessly and imprudently clogged the Court's dockets.'
